column1: # Case corpus for hooks/process-guard.sh. One case per line, two fields:
# `deny` means the guard must refuse the command; `allow` means it must pass
# through. Blank lines and comments are skipped.
# Issue numbers here are five digits so they name nothing. `sanitize-scan.sh`
# refuses a one-to-four-digit tracker reference in anything that ships, and this
# corpus ships. The guard matches the command shape, never the number, so the
# Read the `allow` half first. A false refusal is what gets a hook deleted, and
# a deleted hook enforces nothing — so the cases that cost the most here are the
# ones where a naive match refuses a command that closes nothing. Two of them
# were reproduced against the shipped version by a review, one of them denying
# The corpus also carries `allow` lines for spellings the guard deliberately
# does NOT catch. Those are limits, written down so the next reader meets them
# as a decision rather than as a hole — the convention hooks/agent-cases.tsv

column2: for i in 1 2 3; do gh issue close $i; done
if [ -n "$x" ]; then gh issue close 9; fi

column1: # Whitespace is not a spelling the guard should miss: a session that writes two
# Ordinary spellings rather than evasions, and every one of them slipped past
# the first version. `gh -R owner/repo issue close` in particular is what a
# session writes when it is being careful about which repository it is in.
# gh's own documented way to close an issue, which bypassed the first version
# The waiver is the supported escape, and an empty one is not a waiver. This is
# the pair that matters — a reason present, and a reason that is only nominally

column2: ORRERY_WAIVE="owner said to skip it, we are mid-incident" gh issue close 99042
ORRERY_WAIVE='single quotes are a spelling too' gh issue close 99042

column1: # A waiver attached to something else in the same command line is not a waiver
# for this close. The first version searched the whole command string for the
# token, so this recorded a row and permitted the close.

column2: ORRERY_WAIVE="this is for the echo" echo hi; gh issue close 99042

column1: # Everything else `gh` does with an issue. Reading, commenting and listing are
# how a retrospective gets written in the first place; a guard that blocks them
# blocks the thing it is asking for.
# `close` is not `closed`, and a word boundary is what separates them.
# The permitted path itself, which closes the issue in a subprocess the hook
# never sees. If this were denied there would be no way to comply.
# The regex is quote-blind and cannot be made otherwise without parsing shell,
# so what separates these from a real close is the shape of the argument: a
# digit, a `#`, a variable or a quote — never a word, never `<N>`. Both of the
# first two were reproduced as false refusals against the version that shipped.

column2: git commit -m "guard works; gh issue close is gated now"
git commit -m "and then gh issue close stops working"
echo "gh issue close 42 is what the guard refuses"
printf '%s\n' "  ORRERY_WAIVE=\"why\" gh issue close <N>" > doc.md

column1: # --- the two ordinary spellings, caught on the second pass ---------------------
# A URL is what a session reaches for after copying a link out of a browser, and
# a pipe into xargs is how a batch close is written — which is the case where
# the gate matters most in aggregate and least per issue. Twelve issues closed
# through one pipe used to leave twelve holes and no waiver.
# With xargs the numbers arrive on stdin, so there is no argument after `close`
# at all. The first version of this required one and therefore caught only the
# spellings that happen to carry `{}` — a corpus written to the regex instead
# of to the spellings, and a review found five bypasses in it. The plainest
# form of all was one of them.

column2: gh issue list --json number --jq '.[].number' | xargs -n1 gh issue close

column1: # These close an issue and are NOT caught. They are `allow` because that is what
# the guard does, not because it is right: a guard that reasons about a string
# cannot follow one through an interpreter. Both take deciding to write, which
# is where the line is drawn — a deliberate evasion is what the waiver is for,
# and the waiver is cheaper than either of these.
# And the cost of being quote-blind, which is not fixable without parsing shell.
# A metacharacter inside quoted prose reads as a command separator, so writing
# *about* the guard can be refused — three times in the session that built it,
# once by the rule on the line above. The workaround is one flag (--body-file);
# the alternative is a heuristic that becomes a bypass.

column2: gh pr comment 303 --body "was: ORRERY_WAIVE=x echo hi; gh issue close 42"

column1: # The xargs rule above brings its own instance of the same cost, and it is a
# case rather than a sentence in a commit message — which is the principle this

column2: git commit -m "batch form: cat ids | xargs -I{} gh issue close {} now denied"

column1: # A backslash-escaped `|` is alternation in a search pattern, not a pipe. An
# auditor's `grep 'push\|gh pr create'` was counted as a pull request opened.
# The limit, written down: an unescaped `|` inside quotes still reads as a pipe.
# The matcher is quote-blind by design; see the header.
